bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Cotton price and availability — raw material cost volatility — Cotton is the basic raw material and constitutes the largest component of the cost structure. The MD&A lists volatility in raw material prices among the Company's common risks and states it is of paramount importance that the price and availability of cotton in India remain internationally competitive and assured.
- Cotton import duty policy and the domestic-versus-international cotton price gap — The 11% import duty imposed in 2021 created a significant barrier to imports and left Indian cotton prices materially above international levels, disadvantaging Indian manufacturers against Bangladesh and Vietnam. Duty-free windows have only been granted for limited periods, creating uncertainty that prevents timely procurement decisions. Management explicitly cautions that commodity spinning margins remain sensitive to the gap between domestic and international cotton prices.
- Global brands specifying particular cotton varieties and origins — Buyers increasingly specify the type and origin of cotton (MOT USA, Australian, CME/CMI). If free import of cotton is not permitted, the Company may be unable to offer certain product lines, and the buyer may shift the entire order to another country where the required variety is readily available.
- Trade policy, tariffs and geopolitical disruption to export demand — The MD&A cites geo-political tensions leading to supply chain disruptions and effects on global demand among the Company's common risks. U.S. trade-policy and tariff changes disrupted global sourcing patterns during the year, with brands shifting business to countries perceived to have a more favourable tariff position, adversely impacting export-oriented manufacturers including Vardhman's fabric business.
- Export and geographic concentration in a weak global textile trade — Exports are a large share of turnover and the Company services 60-plus countries, so demand is exposed to the world textile and clothing trade, which showed a poor outlook with most leading exporting countries seeing declines. When U.S. exports slowed, Indian mills redirected to the domestic market, intensifying price competition and pressuring margins across the industry.
- Margin compression from the lag between raw-material cost and product pricing — Fabric margins felt the lag between raw-material costs and fabric pricing, which typically runs about two to three months. A sharp rise in yarn prices coupled with brands' reluctance to absorb costs led to margin compression across the value chain.
- Foreign exchange fluctuation — Forex fluctuations are named in the MD&A among the Company's common business risks, relevant given the substantial share of revenue derived from exports.
- Climate-related physical and transition risk — The Company identifies acute physical risks (floods, heatwaves, storms, wildfires disrupting operations, infrastructure and supply chains), chronic physical risks (changing rainfall, prolonged droughts, rising temperatures), and transition risks spanning policy and regulatory (carbon pricing, disclosure requirements, emissions legislation), market (changing customer demand toward environmentally responsible products), reputational and technology risks (low-carbon investment, asset obsolescence, pace of energy transition). Cotton is a natural raw material whose production is highly dependent on weather conditions.
- Regulatory change, competition, technology obsolescence, talent retention and legal risk — The MD&A's Risk Management section names change in Government regulations, competition, technology obsolescence, retention of talent and legal risk among the common risks. The Board has constituted a Risk Management Committee under the chairmanship of an Independent Director and adopted a Risk Management Policy covering risks that in the Board's opinion may threaten the existence of the Company.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Vardhman is midway through a capital investment programme of approximately Rs 3,660 crore, described by management as one of the most significant expansion cycles in its recent history, spanning spinning and weaving, an entry into technical textiles, fabric processing, garment manufacturing, comprehensive modernisation of existing assets and green energy infrastructure. Capital is deployed across five priorities. In spinning and fabric, a modernisation programme of around Rs 1,200 crore is upgrading existing assets to improve efficiency, cut cost and enable more complex, higher-margin yarns; approximately 35,000 additional spindles were commissioned during FY26, taking spindle count to about 1.25 million. Technical textiles marks the formal entry into a new higher-margin category, focused initially on synthetic functional fabrics such as windcheaters and rain-protective gear at a Phase-I capacity of around 1.5 million metres per month (15 lakh metres per month) at Baddi, Himachal Pradesh, where commercial production commenced on 1st March 2026 with early demand encouraging, including from sportswear brands. In fabric processing, a Rs 350 crore expansion at Vardhman Fabrics, Budhni, Madhya Pradesh added around 31 million metres per annum of processed-fabric capacity and commenced commercial production on 7th March 2026, lifting total fabric processing capacity including technical textiles to about 240 million metres per annum against a weaving base of 1,550 looms. In garments, an investment will increase capacity from 2.2 million to 4.5 million shirts per annum, roughly doubling the production base, with completion targeted in FY27. In green energy, a phased Green Capex programme is replacing coal-fired boilers with biomass and paddy-straw systems, scaling solar generation toward 70 MWp, and adding renewable capacity through a 19.5% stake acquired in Sone Solar Energy One Private Limited, which with developer ASG Holdco Beta Pte Limited is building a 30 MWac (42 MWp) ground-mounted group captive solar plant in Punjab, of which 22.5 MWac is earmarked for Vardhman Textiles and 7.5 MWac for other eligible captive users; the target is 60% green power by FY2027-28. Commissioning is deliberately staggered to match capacity with demand: the Budhni processing line and the technical textiles facility reached commercial production in March 2026 and the bulk of the Green Capex programme is complete, while the garment expansion is targeted for FY27 and modernisation of spinning is to be completed by FY 2026-27. Management states it will raise utilisation of newly commissioned capacity and demonstrate returns before committing to further rounds of expansion. Looking ahead, the Company will evaluate fresh spinning capacity, including a restarted open-end project and planning around the PM MITRA park in Madhya Pradesh, and scale ReNova recycling through additional capacity. The expansion is funded off a reaffirmed CRISIL AA+/Stable rating and a debt-to-equity ratio of around 0.2 times.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Global sourcing is being redrawn as brands and retailers diversify supply away from concentrated geographies toward large, compliant, technologically capable partners — a shift that favours scale players in India
- Structural consolidation of the spinning industry: more than 10-11 million spindles have permanently exited, and China has cut spinning capacity from a peak of around 112 million spindles to about 84 million, tightening supply and rewarding reliable large-scale producers
- The second half of FY 2025-26 marked a turnaround with strengthening order inflows and better industry capacity utilisation; the momentum has continued into FY 2026-27 with improved demand visibility
- Removal of U.S. tariffs restored India's competitiveness in apparel, lifting garment exporters from depressed utilisation back toward full capacity and flowing demand back through the value chain to yarn and fabric
- Chinese yarn offtake from India has risen sharply, with monthly yarn offtake rising from around 90 million kg to nearly 110 million kg
- Free Trade Agreements concluded and upcoming with the UK and EU are expected to reduce tariff disadvantages and improve competitiveness of Indian textile exports; the India-UK FTA in particular can sharpen the competitiveness of Indian fabric and apparel
- Cotton economics are the central margin driver: the 11% import duty and MSP levels kept Indian cotton at a premium to international benchmarks, compressing spinning spreads before they recovered as prices realigned
- Fabric margins lag raw-material costs by about two to three months, managed through selective negotiated price increases and absorbed by integration
- Shift toward processed fabric is expected to yield higher realisations than grey fabric, while technical textiles, value-added fabric and garments carry higher margins than commodity yarn
- Modernisation is expected to lower the cost base; green-energy investment reduces exposure to volatile fossil-fuel costs and meets sustainability expectations embedded in global sourcing
- Sustainability requirements are accelerating demand for recycled, traceable and value-added yarn
- Global apparel consumption continues to rise and premiumisation is accelerating, while brands consolidate supplier bases around quality, compliance and reliability
- Executive sentiment is cautious: McKinsey's State of Fashion 2026 reports 46% of leaders expecting conditions to worsen in 2026, while 25% foresee improvement
- The programme is designed to make the business less cyclical, less commoditised and more profitable across the cycle

Capital is deployed across five priorities. In spinning and fabric, a modernisation programme of around Rs 1,200 crore is upgrading existing assets to improve efficiency, cut cost and enable more complex, higher-margin yarns; approximately 35,000 additional spindles were commissioned during FY26, taking spindle count to about 1.25 million. Technical textiles marks the formal entry into a new higher-margin category, focused initially on synthetic functional fabrics such as windcheaters and rain-protective gear at a Phase-I capacity of around 1.5 million metres per month (15 lakh metres per month) at Baddi, Himachal Pradesh, where commercial production commenced on 1st March 2026 with early demand encouraging, including from sportswear brands. In fabric processing, a Rs 350 crore expansion at Vardhman Fabrics, Budhni, Madhya Pradesh added around 31 million metres per annum of processed-fabric capacity and commenced commercial production on 7th March 2026, lifting total fabric processing capacity including technical textiles to about 240 million metres per annum against a weaving base of 1,550 looms. In garments, an investment will increase capacity from 2.2 million to 4.5 million shirts per annum, roughly doubling the production base, with completion targeted in FY27. In green energy, a phased Green Capex programme is replacing coal-fired boilers with biomass and paddy-straw systems, scaling solar generation toward 70 MWp, and adding renewable capacity through a 19.5% stake acquired in Sone Solar Energy One Private Limited, which with developer ASG Holdco Beta Pte Limited is building a 30 MWac (42 MWp) ground-mounted group captive solar plant in Punjab, of which 22.5 MWac is earmarked for Vardhman Textiles and 7.5 MWac for other eligible captive users; the target is 60% green power by FY2027-28. Commissioning is deliberately staggered to match capacity with demand: the Budhni processing line and the technical textiles facility reached commercial production in March 2026 and the bulk of the Green Capex programme is complete, while the garment expansion is targeted for FY27 and modernisation of spinning is to be completed by FY 2026-27. Management states it will raise utilisation of newly commissioned capacity and demonstrate returns before committing to further rounds of expansion. Looking ahead, the Company will evaluate fresh spinning capacity, including a restarted open-end project and planning around the PM MITRA park in Madhya Pradesh, and scale ReNova recycling through additional capacity. The expansion is funded off a reaffirmed CRISIL AA+/Stable rating and a debt-to-equity ratio of around 0.2 times.

VTL is the best-placed, lowest-cost integrated player to ride a multi-quarter spread recovery plus a 12–18 month FTA-led demand wave.

one_liner.body: Vardhman Textiles is the flagship company of the Vardhman Group and one of India's most extensively vertically integrated textile manufacturers, operating an installed spinning capacity of about 1.25 million spindles alongside weaving, fabric processing and garmenting.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Vardhman converts fibre into yarn, yarn into woven fabric and fabric into finished garments from a single integrated base spanning Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. The product portfolio covers greige and dyed yarns in cotton, polyester, acrylic and blends, speciality yarns including organic cotton, melange, core-spun, gassed mercerised and super-fine variants, woven shirting and trousering fabrics, and finished shirts for premium international brands. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Global sourcing is being redrawn as brands and retailers diversify supply away from concentrated geographies toward large, compliant, technologically capable partners — a shift that favours scale players in India
- Structural consolidation of the spinning industry: more than 10-11 million spindles have permanently exited, and China has cut spinning capacity from a peak of around 112 million spindles to about 84 million, tightening supply and rewarding reliable large-scale producers
- The second half of FY 2025-26 marked a turnaround with strengthening order inflows and better industry capacity utilisation; the momentum has continued into FY 2026-27 with improved demand visibility
- Removal of U.S. tariffs restored India's competitiveness in apparel, lifting garment exporters from depressed utilisation back toward full capacity and flowing demand back through the value chain to yarn and fabric
- Chinese yarn offtake from India has risen sharply, with monthly yarn offtake rising from around 90 million kg to nearly 110 million kg
- Free Trade Agreements concluded and upcoming with the UK and EU are expected to reduce tariff disadvantages and improve competitiveness of Indian textile exports; the India-UK FTA in particular can sharpen the competitiveness of Indian fabric and apparel
- Cotton economics are the central margin driver: the 11% import duty and MSP levels kept Indian cotton at a premium to international benchmarks, compressing spinning spreads before they recovered as prices realigned
- Fabric margins lag raw-material costs by about two to three months, managed through selective negotiated price increases and absorbed by integration
- Shift toward processed fabric is expected to yield higher realisations than grey fabric, while technical textiles, value-added fabric and garments carry higher margins than commodity yarn
- Modernisation is expected to lower the cost base; green-energy investment reduces exposure to volatile fossil-fuel costs and meets sustainability expectations embedded in global sourcing
- Sustainability requirements are accelerating demand for recycled, traceable and value-added yarn
- Global apparel consumption continues to rise and premiumisation is accelerating, while brands consolidate supplier bases around quality, compliance and reliability
- Executive sentiment is cautious: McKinsey's State of Fashion 2026 reports 46% of leaders expecting conditions to worsen in 2026, while 25% foresee improvement
- The programme is designed to make the business less cyclical, less commoditised and more profitable across the cycle

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Vardhman is midway through a capital investment programme of approximately Rs 3,660 crore, described by management as one of the most significant expansion cycles in its recent history, spanning spinning and weaving, an entry into technical textiles, fabric processing, garment manufacturing, comprehensive modernisation of existing assets and green energy infrastructure. Capital is deployed across five priorities. In spinning and fabric, a modernisation programme of around Rs 1,200 crore is upgrading existing assets to improve efficiency, cut cost and enable more complex, higher-margin yarns; approximately 35,000 additional spindles were commissioned during FY26, taking spindle count to about 1.25 million. Technical textiles marks the formal entry into a new higher-margin category, focused initially on synthetic functional fabrics such as windcheaters and rain-protective gear at a Phase-I capacity of around 1.5 million metres per month (15 lakh metres per month) at Baddi, Himachal Pradesh, where commercial production commenced on 1st March 2026 with early demand encouraging, including from sportswear brands. In fabric processing, a Rs 350 crore expansion at Vardhman Fabrics, Budhni, Madhya Pradesh added around 31 million metres per annum of processed-fabric capacity and commenced commercial production on 7th March 2026, lifting total fabric processing capacity including technical textiles to about 240 million metres per annum against a weaving base of 1,550 looms. In garments, an investment will increase capacity from 2.2 million to 4.5 million shirts per annum, roughly doubling the production base, with completion targeted in FY27. In green energy, a phased Green Capex programme is replacing coal-fired boilers with biomass and paddy-straw systems, scaling solar generation toward 70 MWp, and adding renewable capacity through a 19.5% stake acquired in Sone Solar Energy One Private Limited, which with developer ASG Holdco Beta Pte Limited is building a 30 MWac (42 MWp) ground-mounted group captive solar plant in Punjab, of which 22.5 MWac is earmarked for Vardhman Textiles and 7.5 MWac for other eligible captive users; the target is 60% green power by FY2027-28. Commissioning is deliberately staggered to match capacity with demand: the Budhni processing line and the technical textiles facility reached commercial production in March 2026 and the bulk of the Green Capex programme is complete, while the garment expansion is targeted for FY27 and modernisation of spinning is to be completed by FY 2026-27. Management states it will raise utilisation of newly commissioned capacity and demonstrate returns before committing to further rounds of expansion. Looking ahead, the Company will evaluate fresh spinning capacity, including a restarted open-end project and planning around the PM MITRA park in Madhya Pradesh, and scale ReNova recycling through additional capacity. The expansion is funded off a reaffirmed CRISIL AA+/Stable rating and a debt-to-equity ratio of around 0.2 times.

- China officially cutting Xinjiang cotton acreage (shifting to food grains) + spindles 112mn→84mn over 15 yrs → long-term Chinese spinning retreat = durable India tailwind.
- Indian per-farmer cotton output ~5 bales vs thousands in US/Brazil — small landholdings cap productivity; Mission for Cotton Productivity may lift 450→~550 kg/acre (+~20%) but won't reach US/Brazil levels.
- Forex policy: VTL covers rupee same-day on booking exports → Q4 MTM loss already locks in better realisation for FY27 exports at INR94.80.
- Fabric-price lag means Q4 understated true earnings power; Q1 FY27 is the cleaner read.
challenges → beneficiaries:
- ✅ **VTL** — best-placed integrated player; benefits from spread recovery, China pull, consolidation, FTA, fabric value-add, green power.
- ✅ Indian spinning peers (Nitin Spinners, GHCL Textiles, Vardhman-type integrated mills) — same cyclical/structural tailwinds.
- ⭐ Organised spinners able to add capacity into FTA demand (15-month horizon).
- (China/Pakistan/Vietnam/Bangladesh spinning structurally capped — relative loser vs India.)

One-off: ~INR57–58 cr MTM forex loss depressed Q4 EBITDA/PAT (reverses as Q1 FY27 benefit). GM +~300 bps QoQ. Fabric price hikes lag 2–3 months → Q1 FY27 catch-up. Capex: modernization ~90% done; green power live in 1–2 months; PM MITRA land Dec/Jan; open-end project restart. Guidance: Q1 FY27 "far better" for textiles incl VTL; FTA demand ramp ~15 months out.

themes.title: Textiles - apparel/home-textile exports + synthetics
themes.need: India textiles ride three tailwinds at once: China+1 sourcing shifts, the India-UK FTA (signed) + India-EU FTA (advancing), and US tariff normalization - favouring apparel exporters (GOKEX/PGIL/PDSL) and US-heavy home-textile names (WELSPUNLIV/HIMATSEIDE). A second leg = value-added synthetics/recycling (FILATEX, SANATHAN, CENTENKA, GANECOS) and cotton-yarn spread recovery (VTL/NITINSPIN/SPORTKING) plus branded apparel (PAGEIND, ARVIND, RAYMONDLSL).
